why:
phase-456 W2 — what `rclcpp::Subscription<M>::SharedPtr` names. Upstream's is a `std::shared_ptr<Subscription<M>>`; ours is a two-word `{executor, handle_id}` value, and the difference is not an optimisation. A subscription created with a CALLBACK is owned by the Rust executor arena, which holds the `RmwSubscriber`, the rx buffer, the callback and (phase-456 W1) its capture. There is no C++ object for a pointer to point at, and none is made.

What shipped before was a `shared_ptr` aliasing into a heap cell, carrying `take()`, `take_serialized()`, `take_validated()`, `take_sequence()` and `borrow()` -- every one guaranteed to answer `NotInitialized`, because the sample went to the callback. `rclcpp/rclcpp.hpp` said exactly that in a comment while handing the type out. This type is that keep-alive with the failing half removed.

MEASURED (phase-456 W2): the ported corpus calls NOTHING on a subscription handle -- it is stored and dropped. `try_recv` (16), `take` (11) and `take_serialized`/`take_validated` (6) are all POLL-path calls on the out-ref `Subscription<M>`, which this does not change.

W2's cost was that `SharedPtr::element_type` could not be written: naming `Subscription<M>` as the referent would have promised `take()` and friends, which a registration cannot perform. phase-456 W2b REPAID it -- the taking API is `nros::PollSubscription<M>`'s, so `element_type` names `Subscription<M>` again and every operation left on that class is one an arena registration has. Correcting W2's stated reason while repaying it: upstream rclcpp DOES have `Subscription::take`; what it does not have is a caller-owned subscriber, which is what ours is. See `cpp:Subscription::take`.
